result:
The rain had been falling for three days without pause, turning the narrow lanes of the coastal village into shallow rivers that reflected the gray sky like dull mirrors. Mara stood at the window of the rented cottage, her hands wrapped around a mug of tea that had long since gone cold. She watched the water sheet down the glass and thought about the letter that had arrived the morning before the storm began. It was from her sister, written in the careful hand that had not changed since they were girls sharing a bedroom in their parents’ house two hundred miles inland.

The letter spoke of their mother’s declining health, of the garden that no longer bloomed because no one remembered which plants needed which soil, of the way the house itself seemed to be shrinking around the remaining furniture. Mara had read it twice, then folded it and placed it inside the book she was not reading. She had come to the village to finish a translation that was already three weeks overdue, yet the words on her screen remained stubbornly foreign, as if the language itself had decided to withhold its meanings until the weather cleared.

Outside, a fishing boat rocked against its mooring, the hull striking the dock with a dull, rhythmic thud that carried through the walls. Mara counted the impacts without meaning to—seventeen, eighteen—then forced herself to turn away. On the table lay her notebook, open to a page filled with half-sentences and crossed-out phrases. She had intended the trip to be a retreat, a place where the only demands were the ones she set for herself. Instead the rain had become another kind of demand, insistent and without schedule.

She remembered the summer she and her sister had spent here as children, sent to stay with an aunt while their parents argued about money and futures that never quite arrived. The aunt had owned a small shop that sold postcards and fishing line. In the afternoons the girls were allowed to walk as far as the breakwater if they promised to return before the tide turned. Mara had liked the way the stones of the breakwater fitted together, each one chosen and placed by hands that no longer existed. Her sister had preferred the shops, the bright windows, the possibility of something sweet. They had not fought about it then. The difference had seemed small enough to ignore.

Now the difference felt larger. Her sister had stayed near their mother, had learned the names of doctors and the schedules of medications, had become the person who answered the phone when it rang at odd hours. Mara had moved farther away with each job, each city, telling herself that distance was a kind of freedom. The letter made the freedom look like avoidance. She picked up the notebook and wrote a single sentence: I should have gone home last winter. Then she crossed it out because the words sounded like an apology she was not ready to send.

The boat struck the dock again. Mara set the mug down and opened the door. The air outside was thick with salt and the smell of wet wood. She walked to the end of the short path that led to the lane, her shoes darkening at once. No one else was out. The village kept its shutters closed against weather like this; even the bakery had posted a handwritten sign saying it would reopen when the rain eased. Mara stood in the middle of the lane and let the water run into her collar. It was colder than she expected. She thought of the translation waiting on her laptop, of the client who had already sent two polite reminders, of the way her sister’s handwriting had trembled slightly on the final line.

A gull landed on the roof of the cottage opposite and shook its wings. Mara watched it until it flew again, a pale shape against the low cloud. She tried to remember the last time she and her sister had spoken without the subject of their mother rising between them like a third person in the room. It had been years. They exchanged messages about practical things—birthdays, a leak in the roof, the sale of their father’s old car—but the messages never quite became conversations. Mara wondered whether her sister resented the silence or had simply grown used to it, the way one grows used to a door that no longer closes properly.

She turned and walked back toward the cottage, slower now. Inside, she dried her hair with a towel and sat again at the table. The notebook page looked emptier than before. She wrote the sentence a second time, without crossing it out: I should have gone home last winter. Beneath it she added another line, then another, until the page held a short list of things she had postponed. None of the items were dramatic. They were ordinary failures of attention—phone calls not returned, visits shortened, questions left unasked because the answers might have required her to stay longer than she planned.

The rain continued. Mara closed the notebook and opened her laptop. The translation file waited, cursor blinking at the end of an unfinished paragraph. She read the original sentence again, a description of a harbor at dusk, and began to type. The words came slowly, then with more certainty, as if the act of choosing them gave her a small measure of control over the larger choices she had avoided. Outside, the boat kept striking the dock. She no longer counted the sounds. When the light began to fail she switched on the lamp and kept working, the cold tea forgotten beside her, the letter still tucked inside the unread book. By the time full dark arrived she had finished two pages. They were not perfect, but they were done, and for the moment that felt like enough.
